title: Europe 3 of 6 · Central Europe
edition: Europe countries · Six regional lessons · John · November 2026
intro: Welcome to Europe episode three of six. First, I clear the chosen names so we can study a fresh regional group.
Eight places connect the central crossroads and the Alps: Germany, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, Poland, Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary. Liechtenstein uses a labelled supplemental map.

states.name: Germany
lines: Germany is central Europe’s broad northern anchor, south of Denmark and east of the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Poland and Czechia lie along its eastern side.
German reunification took effect on October third, 1990. The Berlin Wall had fallen the previous year, making the two dates related but different.
Remember Germany as a central crossroads between western Europe, the Baltic side and the Alps. Reunification is the historical hook attached to that central position.
states.transition: Let's bring Germany and its neighbours into a closer view.

states.name: Switzerland
lines: Switzerland sits in the Alps, below Germany and between France, Italy and Austria. Liechtenstein is tucked against its eastern side.
Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Its mountain setting holds several language communities within one country.
Picture a multilingual Alpine crossroads. France is west, Italy south, Germany north; keep Switzerland inland, rather than looking for a coast.
states.transition: Let's bring Switzerland and its neighbours into a closer view.

states.name: Liechtenstein
lines: Liechtenstein is the small Alpine country between Switzerland and Austria. The Rhine runs along much of its western boundary beside Switzerland.
It is doubly landlocked: both its neighbours are landlocked too. You must cross at least two national borders to reach an open sea.
Remember the tiny slot between Switzerland and Austria: landlocked neighbours around a landlocked country. This labelled supplemental map shows its actual outline.
states.transition: Let's locate Liechtenstein on a labelled supplemental map, then zoom in to see its outline.
mapFacts: Liechtenstein is the small Alpine country between Switzerland and Austria. The Rhine runs along much of its western boundary beside Switzerland.
It is doubly landlocked: both its neighbours are landlocked too. You must cross at least two national borders to reach an open sea.

states.name: Austria
lines: Austria stretches east from Switzerland and Liechtenstein, below Germany and Czechia. Italy and Slovenia lie to the south, with Hungary toward its eastern end.
Vienna became a major European centre of music, associated with composers including Mozart and Beethoven. The city of music gives Austria a memorable cultural anchor.
Keep Austria as the long Alpine country east of Switzerland. Its eastern end points toward Vienna and the Danube, leading us toward the countries farther east.
states.transition: Let's bring Austria and its neighbours into a closer view.

states.name: Poland
lines: Poland is the broad country east of Germany and north of Czechia and Slovakia. Its northern edge reaches the Baltic; Belarus and Ukraine lie to the east.
Poland regained independence in 1918 after 123 years of partition. Its people and culture continued even while an independent Polish state was absent from the map.
Picture Poland above the Czechia-Slovakia pair, with a Baltic opening at the top. The lost-and-restored state is a historical hook, not a description of today’s borders.
states.transition: Let's bring Poland and its neighbours into a closer view.

states.name: Czechia
lines: Czechia is the inland country below Poland, east of Germany and north of Austria. Slovakia lies immediately to its east.
Charles University in Prague was founded in 1348. Picture an old university city inside this landlocked country, rather than confusing it with a coastal state.
Remember the west-east pair: Czechia, then Slovakia. Czechia touches Germany; Slovakia stretches onward toward Ukraine. Slovenia is a different country farther south.

states.name: Slovakia
lines: Slovakia is the narrow inland country east of Czechia, below Poland and above Hungary. Its eastern tip reaches Ukraine.
Bratislava, its capital, was a coronation city for the Hungarian kingdom between 1563 and 1830. Present-day borders and historical kingdoms do not always line up.
Keep Slovakia above Hungary and east of Czechia. To separate the similar names, remember Slovakia beside Czechia; Slovenia will appear beside the Adriatic countries later.

states.name: Hungary
lines: Hungary lies below Slovakia and east of Austria, in the inland basin crossed by the Danube. Romania is to the east, with Serbia and Croatia toward the south.
Erno Rubik invented his famous rotating cube in Budapest in 1974. The puzzle gives Hungary a colourful memory hook in the middle of this inland group.
Picture the Rubik’s Cube below Slovakia and beside Austria. Keep Hungary away from the coast: it is an inland country with the Danube running through it.

recap: Germany anchors the north; Switzerland and Austria follow the Alps, with tiny Liechtenstein between them. Remember reunification, four languages, the doubly landlocked country, and Vienna’s music.
Farther east, Poland sits above Czechia and Slovakia; Hungary lies below Slovakia. Keep Slovakia beside Czechia, not confused with Slovenia. Those eight places complete our central group.
